title: Node, npm and Express
blurb: The runtime, the module system, middleware, streams and the npm ecosystem — what a fullstack interview expects you to know about the server side of JavaScript.

questions.q: What does Node have that the browser does not?
choices: Filesystem, process, network server sockets, and child processes
Promises and async/await
The event loop
JSON parsing
questions.why: Both run V8 and both have an event loop and promises. Node adds the OS-facing APIs and drops the DOM, window and localStorage — which is why 'window is not defined' shows up during server-side rendering.

questions.q: What is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
choices: dependencies are needed at runtime in production; devDependencies only to build and test
devDependencies are installed globally
dependencies are locked, devDependencies are not
There is no functional difference
questions.why: `npm ci --omit=dev` in a production image skips devDependencies, giving a smaller, faster, less exposed container. Putting TypeScript or a test runner in dependencies is a common slip.

questions.q: What does `package-lock.json` guarantee?
choices: The exact resolved version of every package in the tree, so installs are reproducible
That no package can be malicious
That versions stay within the semver range
Faster installs only
questions.why: Without a lockfile, `^1.2.0` can resolve to a different 1.x on the CI machine than on yours. Commit it, and use `npm ci` in CI — it installs strictly from the lockfile and fails if package.json disagrees.
questions.asked: Follow-up: 'what's the difference between npm install and npm ci?'

questions.q: What does `^1.2.3` allow?
choices: Any 1.x.y at or above 1.2.3 — minor and patch updates, not 2.0.0
Only patch updates
Any version above 1.2.3 including 2.x
Exactly 1.2.3
questions.why: `~1.2.3` is patch-only. Semver's promise is that minor versions are backwards compatible — which holds often enough to be useful and not always enough to skip the lockfile.

questions.q: What is Express middleware?
choices: A function `(req, res, next)` in an ordered chain, each able to handle the request or pass it on
A plugin system for routes
A wrapper around the database
Code that runs after the response is sent
questions.why: Order is everything: a body parser registered after a route means `req.body` is undefined there, and an auth middleware registered after a route does not protect it.

questions.q: Why does this error handler never run?
choices: It is registered before the routes, so nothing downstream can reach it
Error handlers need three parameters, not four
It must be wrapped in try/catch
res.status cannot be used in an error handler
questions.why: Express matches middleware in registration order, and an error handler must come last. It is also identified by having four parameters — dropping `next` turns it into ordinary middleware.

questions.q: In Express 4, why does a rejected promise in an async route handler not reach the error handler?
choices: Express 4 does not catch rejections — you must call next(err) or use a wrapper
Async handlers are not supported at all
The error handler must be async too
It does; the handler is misconfigured
questions.why: The request hangs until it times out, which is worse than a 500. Wrap handlers in an asyncHandler that attaches `.catch(next)`, or move to Express 5, which forwards rejections automatically.
questions.asked: A very practical Express question — this bug produces mysterious hanging requests.

questions.q: What is the difference between CommonJS and ESM in Node?
choices: require is synchronous and dynamic; import is static, asynchronous and needs "type": "module" or .mjs
ESM only works in the browser
CommonJS is deprecated and removed
They can be mixed freely with no caveats
questions.why: Static imports enable tree shaking and top-level await. The friction: `__dirname` does not exist in ESM (use import.meta.url), and importing CJS from ESM works while the reverse needs dynamic import().

questions.q: Why should you stream a large file rather than read it into memory?
choices: A buffer holds the whole file in RAM; a stream processes it in chunks with constant memory
Streams are always faster
fs.readFile cannot handle files over 100MB
Streams compress the data
questions.why: Ten concurrent requests each reading a 500MB file is 5GB of RAM and an OOM kill. Streams also start delivering bytes immediately, so time-to-first-byte improves.

questions.q: What is backpressure in a stream?
choices: The consumer signalling it cannot keep up, so the producer should pause
Errors propagating upstream
The buffer flushing to disk
A retry mechanism
questions.why: Ignore it and you buffer an entire fast source in memory while a slow destination crawls. `pipeline()` handles backpressure and error propagation for you — hand-rolled `.on('data')` loops usually do not.

questions.q: How should configuration reach a Node service?
choices: Environment variables, validated at startup, with secrets from a secret store
A config.json committed to the repo
Hard-coded constants per environment
Command-line flags only
questions.why: Environment config is the twelve-factor default and is what containers and CI expect. Validate at boot and crash loudly — discovering a missing DATABASE_URL at 3am on first request is much worse than at deploy.

questions.q: What happens on an uncaught exception in Node?
choices: The process crashes by default — and letting it crash under a supervisor is usually correct
Node logs it and continues safely
It is caught by the nearest middleware
The event loop restarts
questions.why: After an uncaught exception, application state is unknown. Log it, flush, and exit; let the orchestrator restart a clean process. Using `process.on('uncaughtException')` to keep running is how you get a zombie server.

questions.q: How do you use more than one CPU core in Node?
choices: Run multiple processes (cluster, PM2, or several containers); use worker_threads for CPU-bound work in-process
Node uses all cores automatically
Use more async/await
Increase the thread pool size
questions.why: JavaScript executes on one thread per process. In practice most services scale by running N containers behind a load balancer, which also gives you restarts and rolling deploys for free.

questions.q: What blocks the Node event loop?
choices: Synchronous CPU work or sync I/O like fs.readFileSync — every other request waits
Any await
Database queries
Reading environment variables
questions.why: A single 2-second JSON.parse of a huge payload stalls every concurrent request on that process. Async I/O is fine — it is synchronous computation that hurts.
questions.asked: Then: 'so how would you handle a CPU-heavy endpoint?' — worker thread, queue, or a different runtime.

questions.q: What does a health check endpoint need to do?
choices: Report whether this instance can serve traffic — ideally separating liveness from readiness
Return the app version
Run the full test suite
Always return 200
questions.why: Liveness: is the process wedged and in need of a restart? Readiness: can it serve right now (dependencies reachable, warm-up done)? Conflating them means a brief database blip restarts every pod.

questions.q: Where should request validation happen in an Express app?
choices: At the edge, in middleware or the handler's first lines, before anything touches the database
In the database via constraints only
In the frontend only
Wherever the value is first used
questions.why: Validate once at the boundary and the rest of the code can trust its inputs. Client-side validation is a UX feature, not a security control — anyone can post directly to your API.

questions.q: What is the risk of `npm install` pulling a transitive dependency you never chose?
choices: A compromised or abandoned deep dependency runs with full process privileges — supply chain risk
It only affects install time
npm blocks transitive dependencies by default
There is no risk if the direct dependency is trusted
questions.why: Install scripts and runtime code both execute as your process. Mitigations: audit regularly, pin with a lockfile, prefer fewer and better-maintained dependencies, and consider `--ignore-scripts` in CI.

questions.q: What does `res.json(data)` do that `res.send(JSON.stringify(data))` does not?
choices: Sets Content-Type: application/json and applies configured replacers and escaping
It is faster
It streams the response
Nothing — they are identical
questions.why: Without the header, clients guess — and some will parse a JSON body as text. Small thing, but it is the cause of 'the response is a string' bugs on the client.

questions.q: What is graceful shutdown and why does it matter?
choices: On SIGTERM, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources, then exit
Restarting the process automatically
Flushing logs before a crash
Draining the database connection pool only
questions.why: During a rolling deploy the orchestrator sends SIGTERM and waits. Exiting immediately drops requests mid-flight and can leave transactions open — users see 502s on every deploy.
questions.asked: A strong signal for anyone claiming deployment experience.

questions.q: How should you log in a production Node service?
choices: Structured JSON to stdout, with levels and a request correlation id
console.log to a file the app rotates itself
Only errors, to keep volume down
Full request and response bodies for every call
questions.why: Containers collect stdout; the app should not manage files. Structured logs are queryable. And never log passwords, tokens, card numbers or full request bodies containing them.

questions.q: What does `app.use(express.json())` actually do?
choices: Parses a JSON request body into req.body when Content-Type matches
Serialises all responses as JSON
Validates the body against a schema
Enables JSON support in routes
questions.why: It only acts when the Content-Type is application/json — which is why a request without that header arrives with an empty `req.body` and no error. Set a size limit too; the default allows a large payload.

questions.q: Why is `path.join(__dirname, userInput)` dangerous?
choices: `../../` in the input escapes the intended directory — path traversal
__dirname is undefined in ESM only
It is slow
It does not work on Windows
questions.why: Resolve the path and then verify it still starts with the intended base directory, or map user input to an allowlist of filenames. Never concatenate user input into a filesystem path unchecked.
